name: Collect and receive laboratory specimens
summary: This process gets blood from the patient into the laboratory in a condition fit for testing. Laboratory assistants draw inpatients on an early-morning round and on stat calls, emergency nurses draw ED patients, often through the IV they are starting, and an outpatient collection centre registers patients, re-keys paper requisitions and draws them. Specimen reception scans each tube, checks the label, spins and sorts it and loads it on the analyser line. The main sources of delay and rework are the batching of routine inpatient draws into the early-morning round, patients who are off the unit, hemolysed ED samples drawn through IV catheters, and mislabelled tubes that must be rejected and redrawn.

baseline.org_archetype: A three-site Ontario community hospital corporation of about 640 beds with one core laboratory, stat laboratories at the smaller sites, pneumatic tubes and a laboratory information system interfaced to the hospital information system.
baseline.notes: One case is one collection event (one patient, one draw, several tubes). COVID-19 swabs taken at the assessment centres are not included; they belong to the assessment centre and referral testing processes.

unit_of_work: one specimen collection (one patient draw with its tubes)
trigger: A laboratory order is released in the hospital information system, or an outpatient arrives at the collection centre with a requisition.
end_state: The specimen is accepted and loaded for in-house testing or packed for a reference laboratory, or the collection is cancelled.

volume.seasonality: Busier in the winter respiratory season and on weekdays; the outpatient collection centre runs weekday mornings, and inpatient collection peaks on the 05:00 to 08:00 round.

evidence.note: Laboratory tests rose from 2,597,035 in 2018/19 to 3,220,658 in 2021/22 (216,000 to 268,000 a month); the number of collections assumes about eight reported tests per draw, the author's estimate.

surge.cause: Winter respiratory virus season (influenza and RSV; COVID-19 waves from 2020)

evidence.note: Author's estimate matching the organisation file: more ED visits and admissions during respiratory season raise draws.

roles.title: Medical laboratory assistant (phlebotomy and specimen processing)

evidence.note: Author's estimate: most of the 75 laboratory assistants (headcount, including part-time) work on collection and specimen reception; the rest process referral tests and do clerical work.
Author's estimate: about 9,000 ED draws a month at about 8 minutes each including sending, about 9 FTE spread across 380 ED nurses.
Author's estimate: line draws and redraws on the inpatient units.
Author's estimate: outpatient collection centre registration at three sites.

systems.name: Hospital information system (electronic patient record with ADT, order entry, results, eMAR and clinical documentation)
Automated chemistry and hematology analyser lines with middleware
Email, telephone, pagers and wireless phones
Safety incident and complaints reporting system

resources.name: Pneumatic tube system (one network per hospital)

steps.name: Release order to collection lists
steps.description: When a physician or nurse enters a laboratory order in the hospital information system, the interface creates the order in the laboratory information system, assigns an accession number and either prints barcode labels at the ordering location or adds the draw to the phlebotomy collection list for the unit and time requested.
outputs: barcode labels or collection list entry

next.condition: routine inpatient draw for the early-morning round
outpatient with a requisition at the collection centre

evidence.note: Split of collections by source is the author's estimate: about 13,000 ED visits a month with blood work for roughly half plus repeat draws, about 520 occupied acute beds drawn about once a day, and outpatient, pre-admission and clinic draws for the rest.

steps.name: Draw ED blood and label at bedside
steps.description: The emergency nurse checks the patient's wristband against the printed labels using two identifiers, draws the tubes in order of draw, often through the IV catheter while starting the line, labels each tube at the bedside and initials the collection time.

error.defect_description: Hemolysed sample from an IV-start draw (about 6%) or a tube labelled away from the bedside or with the wrong patient's label (about 1%).

control.basis: Accreditation Canada Required Organizational Practice on client identification: two person-specific identifiers before any procedure, labels applied in the presence of the patient

evidence.note: ED hemolysis rate of 5.8% in an Ontario tertiary ED (fernandes2004); drawing through IV starts rather than straight-needle venipuncture raises hemolysis about six-fold (risk ratio 0.16 for straight needle, heyer2012). Draw time and wait are author estimates.

steps.name: Send ED tubes by pneumatic tube
steps.description: The nurse or a patient care assistant bags the tubes with the requisition, places the carrier in the ED pneumatic tube station and keys the laboratory destination; stat tubes go straight away rather than waiting for a batch.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common Ontario hospital practice: most sites send ED specimens by pneumatic tube.

steps.name: Dispatch MLA to stat or timed draw
steps.description: The laboratory assistant assigned to inpatient stat draws picks up the collection label printed in the laboratory or the page from the unit, groups it with any other pending stat draws on the same floor and sets off; timed draws such as drug levels wait for their scheduled time.

evidence.note: Author's estimate: inpatient stat draws are usually collected within 15 to 45 minutes; timed draws wait for the scheduled time.

steps.name: Prepare early-morning collection round
steps.description: Before the round starts at about 05:00 the laboratory assistant prints the collection list and labels for the assigned units, sorts them by room, stocks the tray with tubes and needles and checks for special handling such as tubes on ice or fasting draws.

evidence.note: Author's estimate: routine inpatient tests ordered during the day and evening are collected on the early-morning round so results are back for physician rounds; the wait runs from order entry to the round.

steps.name: Walk to unit and patient room
steps.description: The laboratory assistant walks or takes the elevator to the unit, checks with the nurse for patients in isolation or off the unit and goes from room to room with the tray, doing hand hygiene and putting on PPE where signage requires it.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of travel and PPE time per patient on a round; stat draws need a dedicated trip and sit at the high end.

steps.name: Identify patient and check order
steps.description: The assistant asks the patient to state full name and date of birth, compares them and the wristband hospital number with the label and collection list, and confirms fasting status or timing; patients who are off the unit, refuse or have been discharged are recorded in the list.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada Required Organizational Practice on client identification (two identifiers)

next.condition: patient off the unit or unavailable; redraw later
patient discharged, transferred or specimen already collected by someone else

evidence.note: In 683 institutions, 4.9% of inpatient phlebotomy requests were not attempted by the assigned phlebotomist: patient unavailable 1.4%, transferred or discharged 0.9%, already collected by someone else 0.7% (howanitz1994; older US data used as the best available proxy).

steps.name: Perform venipuncture and label tubes
steps.description: The assistant applies the tourniquet, selects a vein, draws the tubes in the correct order of draw and volume, applies pressure and labels each tube at the bedside with the barcode label, writing collection time and initials before leaving the room.

error.defect_description: Tube labelled after leaving the room or wrong tube or volume (about 0.3%), or hemolysis or clotting from a difficult draw (about 1.5%).

control.basis: Accreditation Canada client identification ROP; IQMH (Ontario laboratory accreditation) requirements for labelling at the time of collection

next.condition: unsuccessful or partial draw; nurse draws from a line

evidence.note: 93.2% of inpatient requests were successful venipunctures, 1.6% unsuccessful and 0.4% partially successful (howanitz1994). Minutes per draw are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Nurse draws from central line
steps.description: When the assistant cannot get a sample, the patient's nurse draws it from a central or arterial line after discarding the dead-space volume, labels the tubes at the bedside and sends them; the assistant documents the failed attempt.

error.defect_description: Sample diluted or contaminated with infusion fluid, or labelled away from the bedside.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada client identification ROP (two identifiers)

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice for difficult draws and patients with central lines.

steps.name: Send inpatient tubes to the laboratory
steps.description: The assistant sends stat tubes from the unit's pneumatic tube station straight away; on the early-morning round, tubes collect in the tray and go down in a few carriers or are carried back when the round ends.

evidence.note: Author's estimate: round tubes wait in the tray until a carrier is full or the round ends.

steps.name: Register outpatient and validate health card
steps.description: The registration clerk at the outpatient collection centre takes a number, scans or types the health card number, validates it online, confirms address and family physician and creates or updates the outpatient visit so that labels can be printed.

error.defect_description: Registration under the wrong existing patient record (duplicate or overlay).

control.basis: Hospital registration policy and Ministry of Health eligibility check (health card validation)

evidence.note: Author's estimate of outpatient collection centre practice; waiting times vary with the morning rush.

steps.name: Key requisition tests into the LIS
steps.description: The laboratory assistant reads the paper requisition from the community physician or clinic, enters each requested test and the ordering and copy-to physicians in the laboratory information system and prints the barcode labels for the tubes.

error.defect_description: Test missed or wrong test or wrong copy-to physician keyed from a handwritten requisition.

evidence.note: Author's estimate: in 2019-2022 most outpatient requisitions arrived on paper and were re-keyed.

steps.name: Draw outpatient blood in collection centre
steps.description: The assistant calls the patient to a draw chair, confirms name and date of birth against the labels, performs the venipuncture, labels the tubes in front of the patient and gives any instructions for urine or stool containers.

error.defect_description: Hemolysed, clotted or short sample (about 1%) or a labelling error (about 0.2%).

control.basis: Accreditation Canada client identification ROP; IQMH labelling requirements

evidence.note: Author's estimate; outpatient draws are faster than inpatient draws because patients are seated and mobile.

steps.name: Carry collection-centre batch to core lab
steps.description: Every 20 to 30 minutes an assistant carries the rack of collection-centre tubes, with any urine containers, to specimen reception in the core laboratory or sends it by tube station when the centre is on another floor.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; minutes are per collection, a share of one trip carrying about 15 patients' tubes.

steps.name: Receive and check specimen at reception
steps.description: At specimen reception the laboratory assistant unpacks the carrier, scans each tube to record receipt time in the laboratory information system and compares the label with the order: two identifiers, collection time, collector and correct tube type.

control.basis: Laboratory and Specimen Collection Centre Licensing Act (Ontario) and IQMH accreditation requirements for specimen acceptance and rejection criteria

evidence.note: Author's estimate of the label rejection share; transit wait covers the pneumatic tube or carried tray.

steps.name: Centrifuge, inspect and sort specimens
steps.description: The assistant loads serum and plasma tubes into the centrifuge, inspects the spun samples for visible hemolysis, clots or short volume, and sorts tubes by bench: automation line, hematology, coagulation, manual bench or referral.

next.condition: some tests go to a reference laboratory
visibly hemolysed, clotted or insufficient sample rejected

evidence.note: Hemolysed samples are up to 3.3% of routine samples, with a 2% ASCP benchmark (heyer2012); ED rate 5.8% (fernandes2004). The 3% rejection share blends a higher ED rate with lower inpatient and outpatient rates.

steps.name: Aliquot and package referral tests
steps.description: For tests not done in house, the assistant pours off aliquots into labelled transport tubes, prints the reference laboratory requisition or manifest, packs specimens at the right temperature and places them in the courier box for the scheduled pick-up.

error.defect_description: Aliquot mislabelled or stored at the wrong temperature.

next.condition: all tests on this collection are referral tests

evidence.note: Author's estimate; Public Health Ontario and reference laboratories receive specimens by scheduled courier.

steps.name: Load tubes onto the analyser line
steps.description: The assistant places the sorted tubes in the input module of the automated line or delivers racks to the hematology and coagulation benches, putting stat tubes in the priority lane so they are sampled first.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Reject specimen and request recollection
steps.description: The assistant cancels the affected tests in the laboratory information system with the rejection reason, adds a comment visible on the chart and phones the unit nurse, ED or collection centre to ask for a new specimen.

next.condition: test no longer needed or patient has left

evidence.note: Author's estimate of who redraws and of the share of tests that are dropped rather than redrawn.

steps.name: Record mislabelled specimen as an incident
steps.description: For an unlabelled or mislabelled specimen the assistant logs a safety incident in the incident reporting system naming the collecting area, so that the unit manager and laboratory manager can follow up, then proceeds to reject the specimen.

control.basis: Accreditation Canada patient safety incident management requirements; hospital incident reporting policy

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice; mislabelled specimens are treated as near misses.

exceptions.name: Hemolysed ED sample
exceptions.description: An ED sample drawn through an IV start is visibly hemolysed after spinning; the tests are cancelled and the nurse redraws, adding 30 to 90 minutes to the ED result.

exceptions.name: Mislabelled or unlabelled tube
exceptions.description: Reception finds a label that does not match the order or no label; an incident is logged and the specimen must be redrawn because it cannot be relabelled.

exceptions.name: Patient off the unit on the round
exceptions.description: The patient is in imaging, dialysis or the OR when the assistant arrives; the draw is retried later as a stat-style trip.

exceptions.name: Failed venipuncture
exceptions.description: The assistant cannot obtain blood and the nurse draws it from a central line.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from order release to specimen accepted in the laboratory
benchmarks.population: All collections in a community hospital; routine inpatient draws wait for the early-morning round, ED and stat draws arrive within about an hour

evidence.note: Author's estimate built from the source mix: ED draws reach the laboratory in about 30 to 45 minutes, outpatient and stat draws in about 60 to 90 minutes, and about 40% of draws wait for the early-morning round, so the median falls in the slower part of the fast group. No published order-to-receipt distribution for a comparable hospital was found.

benchmarks.population: Academic tertiary ED in Hamilton, Ontario

benchmarks.unit: share of routine samples received (upper value); ASCP benchmark 0.02
share of inpatient requests with successful venipuncture

evidence.note: Unsuccessful 1.6%, partial 0.4%, not attempted 4.9%.

pain_points.description: Routine inpatient draws are batched into one early-morning round, so tests ordered in the afternoon wait many hours and the round itself is a staffing peak.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common hospital practice.

pain_points.description: ED nurses draw through IV catheters to save a second needle stick, which raises hemolysis and leads to redraws and delayed potassium results.

evidence.note: Straight-needle venipuncture cuts hemolysis by about 84% (risk ratio 0.16); the Ontario ED study found 5.8% hemolysis.

pain_points.description: Outpatient paper requisitions are re-keyed into the laboratory system, with transcription errors and copy-to physicians missed.

evidence.note: Author's estimate for 2019-2022, before wide use of electronic outpatient ordering.

pain_points.description: Patients who are off the unit or already drawn waste a trip and push the draw later.

evidence.note: 4.9% of inpatient requests not attempted, mostly for administrative reasons.

assumptions: One case is one collection event; a collection carries several tubes and on average about eight reported tests, so collections are about one-eighth of the test count.
Routine inpatient draws are taken on an early-morning round; the 120 to 960 minute batch wait at s05 runs from order entry to the start of the round.
ED nurses, not laboratory assistants, draw most ED blood, as is common in Ontario community EDs; some sites may place assistants in the ED during the day.
Specimen reception and processing by laboratory assistants is included here; analysis starts in the laboratory testing process when tubes are on the line.
Rejection for hemolysis is modelled at visual inspection after spinning; hemolysis detected by the analyser's index is handled in the laboratory testing process.

Simulated median cycle time is dominated by ED, stat and outpatient draws that reach the laboratory within an hour; the 90th percentile reflects the early-morning round. The benchmark is an estimate, not a measured distribution.
Staffing: stated FTE includes laboratory assistants' time on the round that is not tied to a single collection (tray stocking, waiting for elevators); the touch-time check is close to the stated FTE.

Simulated median cycle time (about 0.09 days) is about 1.5 times the estimated 0.06 days: queues at outpatient registration and the wait for stat inpatient draws make up the gap. Neither figure is measured, so the gap was left rather than tuned away.
Loaded costs come from the organisation file.

Organisation file corrected on 2026-11-24: dialysis nurses draw the monthly blood work themselves and send specimens straight to the laboratory (hosp-med-hemodialysis), so med-hemodialysis no longer triggers collection; its 4% share is spread over the other sources.
